start_method: indoor start
bloom_color: mix: red, orange, yellow, pink, white, lilac, lime, wine
overwintering_method: Annual everywhere — pull plants after frost. Save seeds by fermenting if desired.
variety_notes: Standard for specialty cut flower growers; endorsed by the Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers (ASCFG). Bred by Ernst Benary, a German seed company founded 1843. Densely petaled double flowers with a high percentage of doubles. Disease-resistant compared to other zinnias. Holds up well in summer heat and rain. Harvest when stem is stiff (wiggle test — if the stem bends, not ready). Do NOT refrigerate. Add a few drops of bleach to vase water to combat murky water.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Harris Seeds; Seed Savers Exchange; Uprising Seeds; Nature & Nurture Seeds
source_notes: Floret Flowers is the authoritative cut flower source (Erin Benzakein wrote the defining specialty cut flower book). All sources agreed on fundamentals.

start_method: tuber
bloom_color: cream-blush-champagne
overwintering_method: Dig tubers 1-2 weeks after first killing frost. Rinse soil, dry 24 hours, store in vermiculite or peat in a cool dark high-humidity location (crawl space or basement). Divide in spring before planting.
variety_notes: Most requested dahlia variety in the floral industry. Dinnerplate form (informal decorative). Massive ruffled blooms resemble pastel silk pillows; wedding industry staple. Stake at planting — blooms are heavy. Harvest when 3/4 open (dahlias do not continue opening after cut). Hot water treatment improves vase life (sear stems in 160-180F water for 1 hour). One tuber produces up to a dozen tubers per season.
sources: Floret Library; White Flower Farm; Longfield Gardens; Sierra Flower Farm; DutchGrown; Bleeding Heart Flower Farm; The Kokoro Garden; Pith + Vigor
source_notes: Vase life shorter than most cut flowers at 4-5 days — worth flagging to users. Bloom timing is notoriously unreliable (pro grower The Kokoro Garden cautions against promising dates).

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: salmon pink
overwintering_method: Annual everywhere — pull plants after frost
variety_notes: Oklahoma series has the highest percentage of reliable double blooms in cutting zinnias — more consistent than Benary's Giants or Zinderella series. Smaller 2-3" blooms on 30" stems — excellent "filler" companion to larger focal flowers. Mildew-resistant. Extremely prolific — single plant can yield a dozen stems at a time. Cooler pastel salmon color works with most color palettes.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; The Kokoro Garden; Lynsey Taulbee; Red Dirt Ramblings
source_notes: Flower farmers universally cite Oklahoma series for reliability; Benary's Giant for size/drama; Queen series for unique colors.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: dusty rose center fading to lime-green outer petals
overwintering_method: Annual everywhere — pull plants after frost
variety_notes: Queen/Queeny series has the most unique sophisticated color palette in zinnias — antique rose, plum, eggplant, lime blushes. Customer favorite for bouquets — the unusual coloration stands out. Not always fully double (some singles appear). Smaller 2-3" blooms on good-length stems. Works in Victorian/moody color palettes.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; The Kokoro Garden; Lynsey Taulbee
source_notes: Queen Red Lime specifically is often cited as THE standout zinnia for unique coloring.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: Granny Smith apple green
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: The iconic "green flower" — visually striking in mixed bouquets. Densely packed petals. Low mildew susceptibility. One of the tallest and strongest-stemmed zinnias (36-48"). 4-6" dahlia-like blooms. Part of Benary's Giant series bred for cut flower production.
sources: Floret Library; Hoss Tools; Territorial Seed; Epic Gardening
source_notes: Green flowers are uncommon and highly sought after for designer work.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: peach blush with scabiosa-like pincushion center
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Scabiosa-flowered zinnia with distinctive "pincushion" bicolor center. Unique novelty appeal. Variable form — not always fully scabiosa-shaped (some singles and partial doubles appear). Lower germination and less vigor than Benary's or Oklahoma. Grow several plants to get a few good blooms. Prized by designers for its cottage-garden character.
source_notes: Inconsistent form is well-documented — set user expectations accordingly.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: soft blush pink
overwintering_method: Annual — but reseeds readily in warm climates
variety_notes: Fused fluted petals form a distinctive "teacup" shape — petals look cut with pinking shears. Palm-sized blooms. Floret favorite and widely praised. Plants grow to 4 feet — stake or net for support. Harvest when buds just cracking open for best vase life. Extremely productive — more you cut, more you get. Bury stems deep like tomatoes for stronger roots and less flopping.
sources: Floret Library; Floret Flower Farm; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Floret blog
source_notes: Single plants described as "flower bushes" by growers — very productive. Vase life is short-term limitation.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: mix: rose, blush, cranberry, white
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Double-flowered form — fluffier and longer-lasting than single cosmos. Earlier to bloom than Cupcakes (75 vs 90 days). Shorter plants (3-4 ft) than some cosmos. Mix gives color variety from one packet. Harvest when half-open for best vase life on doubles.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Floret blog
source_notes: Double forms last slightly longer in vase than singles.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow after frost
bloom_color: pastel mix: pink, rose, white, carmine with bicolors
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Distinctive tubular/fluted petals resembling seashells — unique form. Single-flowered (not double). Large showy blooms in pastel mix. Strong producer. Adds unusual texture to bouquets. Tied with Purity as classic cosmos varieties.
source_notes: Fluted/tubular petal form is the defining character.

start_method: indoor start or direct sow
bloom_color: deep ruby red fading to dusty pink with age
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Uniquely dark cosmos — almost red/burgundy at full bloom, fading through rose and blush as flowers age. Each flower shows multiple colors simultaneously on the plant. Customer favorite for moody/autumn bouquets. Works beautifully with Queen Red Lime zinnias and dahlias.
source_notes: One of the few truly red cosmos — fills a niche in most color palettes.

start_method: indoor start 10-12 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: bronze, peach, pink, purple, red, white, yellow
overwintering_method: In zones 7+ with mulch, plants may survive winter and bloom earlier next year. Treat as annual in colder zones. Fall planting in Southern climates (overwinter with protection) yields longest stems.
variety_notes: OPEN-FACED azalea-flowered snapdragon — no "jaws" to snap. Tall spires (30-42") with dozens of florets. Chantilly is a Group II snapdragon (cool-season tolerant). Extremely long vase life (up to 2 weeks). Flowers from bottom up — harvest when 1/3 to 1/2 open. Pinch at 6" for branching. Cool-season flower — plant in spring (zone 5-7) or fall-overwinter (zone 7-9) for best stem length.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Sakata Ornamentals
source_notes: Snapdragon Group I/II/III/IV classification refers to temperature and daylength response — Group II (Chantilly, Madame Butterfly) is most adaptable to home gardens.

start_method: indoor start 10-12 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: red, rose, yellow, bronze, white
overwintering_method: Treat as annual in cold zones; may overwinter in zone 7+
variety_notes: Double-azalea-flowered snapdragon — fully doubled open-faced blooms. Showy "ruffled" look. Group II (cool-season). Slightly shorter than Chantilly. Long vase life. Excellent alternative when you want doubles instead of the more architectural single-flowered Chantilly.
source_notes: Double-flowered form is the main difference from single Chantilly.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: bronze, cherry, pink, red, yellow, white
overwintering_method: Treat as annual in cold zones
variety_notes: Traditional "snapping jaws" snapdragon — the classic form children love to play with. Group III (heat-tolerant) — better for summer bloom in warm climates where Chantilly/Madame Butterfly struggle. Tall strong stems. Solid colors with traditional snapdragon form. Workhorse cutting variety.
source_notes: Heat tolerance (Group III) makes this the summer snap for mid-Atlantic and Southern gardeners.

start_method: indoor start 10-12 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: soft pink with cream throat
overwintering_method: Requires overwintering in zone 7+ for best stems — these are Group IV long-day snapdragons
variety_notes: Group IV snapdragon — requires long days to flower. Commercial cut-flower quality — tallest stems (36-48"). Single central spike (not branching) — cut the main stem as the entire harvest. Must be fall-planted and overwintered in zone 7+ for proper flowering. Not suitable for spring planting in northern climates. Professional-grade choice for market growers.
source_notes: Group IV requires specific timing — not a beginner variety. Single-cut habit is important to understand.

start_method: direct sow after frost
bloom_color: deep golden orange with dark center
overwintering_method: Annual — pull plants after harvest
variety_notes: THE benchmark commercial cut flower sunflower. POLLENLESS — F1 hybrid that does not shed pollen, so no mess on tablecloths and longer vase life. Single-stem (not branching) — one plant produces one flower. Succession plant every 7-10 days for continuous harvest. ProCut series bred specifically for cut flower production. Uniform timing makes bulk harvesting easy.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Sakata Ornamentals
source_notes: Pollenless (male-sterile) is the critical feature separating commercial cut flower sunflowers from home garden types — no yellow pollen stains.

start_method: direct sow
bloom_color: creamy white with dark chocolate center
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Pollenless white/cream sunflower. Part of ProCut series — reliable uniform single-stem production. Dark chocolate center provides striking contrast. White sunflowers are rare — designers love them for wedding work. Succession plant every 7-10 days.
source_notes: White/cream sunflower niche — premium variety for floral designers.

start_method: direct sow
bloom_color: mix: yellow, gold, mahogany, bronze, bicolors
overwintering_method: Annual — leave seed heads for birds if desired
variety_notes: BRANCHING multi-stem sunflower — one plant produces 6-10 smaller blooms over the season. Heirloom. Rich autumn color palette: yellows, golds, bronzes, mahogany, bicolors. NOT pollenless — classic sunflower that sheds pollen. Shorter vase life than pollenless types. Great for pollinators and seed-saving. Good choice when you want one planting that produces all summer rather than succession planting.
sources: Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Branching habit is trade-off: one planting vs many, but pollen and shorter vase life.

start_method: direct sow
bloom_color: bright golden yellow
overwintering_method: Annual
variety_notes: Fully DOUBLE fluffy sunflower — looks like a pom-pom or dahlia. Dwarf plant (only 2-3 feet tall) — excellent for small spaces, containers, and children's gardens. No visible central disk — all petals. Branching. Bright cheery color. Short-stemmed limits cut flower use but perfect for kids and container growing.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; Baker Creek
source_notes: Dwarf form for containers and children's gardens — not a typical cut flower due to short stems.

start_method: direct sow
bloom_color: classic golden yellow with brown center
overwintering_method: Annual — harvest seed heads for birds or replant
variety_notes: Classic giant heirloom sunflower — 8-12 feet tall, 10-16 inch flower heads. Not primarily a cut flower (too big for most vases) but grown for seeds and as a garden showpiece. Heavy seed production — excellent for wildlife and human snacking. Single massive flower per plant. Support in windy areas.
sources: Baker Creek; Burpee; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Primarily a seed/showpiece variety — included for completeness of sunflower choices.

start_method: plant tubers after frost (soil 60F+)
bloom_color: warm bronze-copper
overwintering_method: Dig tubers 1-2 weeks after killing frost. Rinse, dry 24 hours, divide if needed, store in vermiculite/peat moss in cool dark humid location (40-50F).
variety_notes: BALL dahlia form — tightly packed round blooms, much longer vase life than dinnerplates. Warm copper-bronze color pairs with everything. Prolific bloomer. Ball-form dahlias are the workhorse cut flower dahlias — reliable, productive, long-lasting in vase. 3-4" perfect round form.
sources: Floret Library; Longfield Gardens; Swan Island Dahlias
source_notes: Ball form = longer vase life than dinnerplate form. Essential distinction for cutting garden.

start_method: plant tubers after frost
bloom_color: soft pink
overwintering_method: Dig and store tubers as with all dahlias
variety_notes: Pom-pom / miniature ball form — small 2-3" perfect spheres. Wildly popular with designers — works in everything from bridal bouquets to casual arrangements. Long stems relative to bloom size. Extremely prolific. One of the most reliable and easy-to-use dahlias for beginners.
source_notes: Pom-pom form has smallest blooms but highest stem count per plant.

start_method: plant tubers after frost
bloom_color: coppery peach-pink with golden undertones
overwintering_method: Dig and store tubers
variety_notes: DINNERPLATE size informal decorative dahlia. Massive 7-9" blooms in warm antique coppery-peach tones. Customer favorite for autumn weddings. Stake at planting — heavy blooms need support. Shorter vase life than ball dahlias (4-5 days vs 7+) — the trade-off for drama.
sources: Floret Library; Swan Island Dahlias; Longfield Gardens
source_notes: Dinnerplate form is dramatic but short-lived — manage customer expectations.

start_method: plant tubers after frost
bloom_color: swirling blend of peach, pink, lavender
overwintering_method: Dig and store tubers
variety_notes: Dinnerplate informal decorative dahlia with swirling pastel coloration — no two flowers identical. Wedding industry darling. Large 6-9" blooms. Strong stems. Productive for a dinnerplate. Second only to Café au Lait in floral designer popularity for weddings.
source_notes: Color variability within the variety is a feature, not a bug — appeals to designers.

sun_requirement: full sun (part afternoon shade in hot zones)
start_method: soak seeds 24 hrs; indoor start 10-12 wks before last frost OR fall-plant in mild zones
bloom_color: cream with lavender-purple edges (deepens with age)
overwintering_method: Sweet peas are cool-season annuals; hot weather ends bloom. Zone 7+: fall-plant seeds for spring blooms. Zone 3-6: spring-plant after soaking seeds, pinch early, trellis at planting.
variety_notes: Bred by Dr. Keith Hammett — marries old-fashioned strong fragrance with modern Spencer-type large ruffled blooms. THE most fragrant sweet pea available. Also sold as "High Scent" / "King's High Scent" / "Hi-Scent." 6-8 ft climbing vines need strong trellis. Harvest when 2+ unopened buds at tip. POISONOUS if ingested — caution with kids and pets (not the same as garden pea). Shorter vase life the trade-off for fragrance.
sources: Floret Library; Renee's Garden; Uprising Seeds; Fedco; Deep Harvest Farm; Burfoot Flowers; Sweet Pea Gardens
source_notes: Multiple names for the same Hammett-bred variety. Strongly fragrant sweet peas are a category where this is the clear leader.

sun_requirement: full sun (afternoon shade in hot zones)
start_method: soak seeds; indoor start 10-12 wks before last frost
bloom_color: stormy purple-grey with darker flush
overwintering_method: Cool-season — see other sweet peas
variety_notes: Modern Spencer sweet pea with unique "stormy" grey-purple coloring. Huge fluttery blooms on 12"+ stems. Little to no fragrance — the trade-off modern Spencers make for bloom size and color. Pairs beautifully with April in Paris for combined scent + drama. Designer favorite for moody palette work.
source_notes: Modern Spencers = large ruffled blooms with reduced scent vs. old-fashioned Grandifloras.

sun_requirement: full sun (afternoon shade in hot zones)
start_method: soak seeds; indoor start 10-12 wks before last frost
bloom_color: cream with pink picotee edges
overwintering_method: Cool-season annual — see April in Paris
variety_notes: Cream flowers with warm pink picotee edging. Modern Spencer form. Good fragrance (stronger than Nimbus, not as intense as April in Paris). Long stems. Beloved wedding variety for the romantic cream-and-pink palette.
source_notes: Classic wedding palette choice.

start_method: indoor start 4-6 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: crimson, pink, orange, yellow, cream
overwintering_method: Annual; dries beautifully — harvest and hang upside down for winter arrangements
variety_notes: Classic "cockscomb" / brain-shaped ruffled celosia. Heat-LOVING — thrives in hot humid weather where other flowers fade. Very long vase life (10-14 days fresh, effectively forever dry). Needs long warm growing season — start indoors. Color holds well when dried. Unique textural element unlike anything else. Cut-and-come-again if side shoots encouraged.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Territorial Seed
source_notes: Three celosia categories: crested (cockscomb brains), plumed (feathery plumes), and wheat (spike form). All grow similarly.

start_method: indoor start 4-6 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: available in bright red, pink, yellow, orange, cream
overwintering_method: Annual; excellent for drying
variety_notes: Plumed/feathery celosia form — fluffy upright plumes rather than brain-shaped crests. Sunday series is specifically bred for cut flower production with tall strong stems. Heat-loving. Pinch early for branching. Lasts extraordinarily long in vase. Dries to near-identical color. Versatile in bouquets.
source_notes: Sunday series is commercial cut-flower bred; consumer-grade Century series is shorter and bushier.

start_method: indoor start
bloom_color: soft pink fading to silver-white at tips
overwintering_method: Annual; dries excellently
variety_notes: Wheat-type celosia — narrow upright spikes like wheat heads, softer texture than crested or plumed. Soft pink with silvery tips — resembles flamingo feathers. Tall strong stems. Natural "prairie" aesthetic. Pairs with grasses and wildflower-style arrangements. Dries beautifully.
source_notes: Wheat celosia is less common — Flamingo Feather is the most popular cut flower version.

start_method: direct sow early spring or fall (hardy)
bloom_color: deep maroon-black
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — can survive winter in zones 7+ if fall-planted; otherwise early spring sow
variety_notes: Also called Cornflower. "Black Ball" is the nearly-black variety — rare dark flower highly prized by designers. Classic cottage garden flower. Cool-season hardy annual — germinates in cool soil, tolerates frost. Plants bolt in heat. Fall-plant in zones 7+ for spring bloom. Reseeds reliably.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: Hardy annuals like bachelor's button should be planted EARLY — they struggle in heat.

start_method: indoor start 6-8 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: dusty rose, rusty red, cream, caramel, bronze
overwintering_method: Short-lived perennial in zones 3-7 (often only 1-2 years); grown as annual in most climates for cut flowers
variety_notes: Remarkable color palette for a rudbeckia — antique muted tones (dusty rose, rust, cream, caramel) very unlike typical bright yellow black-eyed Susans. Bred specifically for cut flowers. Productive heat-tolerant bloomer from mid-summer through frost. Pinch early for branching. Customer favorite for autumn wedding palettes.
source_notes: Breaks from traditional yellow-rudbeckia expectations — notable for distinctive color range.

start_method: indoor start
bloom_color: classic golden yellow with dark brown center
overwintering_method: Often grown as annual; may overwinter in zones 3-7
variety_notes: 1995 AAS winner. Enormous 6-9" golden-yellow daisies with dark centers. Dramatic size — single stems fill a vase. Classic black-eyed Susan appearance but supersized. Heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant. Heavy producer. A cottage-garden and cutting-garden staple.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Burpee; All-America Selections
source_notes: The "grande" traditional black-eyed Susan — dramatically larger than wild Rudbeckia hirta.

start_method: indoor start 4-6 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: warm copper-red with golden center
overwintering_method: Annual; premier drying flower — hang upside down to dry (holds color and form indefinitely)
variety_notes: Also called Everlasting. Papery straw-textured petals that NEVER WILT — flowers feel dry even fresh on plant. Retain full color and shape when dried. Long vase life fresh (10-14 days). Premier dried flower. Productive and heat-tolerant. Essential component for dried wreaths and winter arrangements.
source_notes: Straw-textured petals are unique — can't be confused with anything else.

start_method: indoor start 6-8 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: purple, blue, pink, white, yellow, apricot
overwintering_method: Annual in cold zones; tender perennial in zone 8+. Excellent drying flower — holds color for months.
variety_notes: QIS (Quick Improved Statice) series bred for cut flower production. Papery calyxes in bright colors with tiny white interior flowers. Long vase life. THE classic dried flower for color retention. Heat-tolerant. Branching plants produce many stems. Drought-tolerant once established.
source_notes: Statice is a bridge between fresh and dried flowers — works equally well for both.

start_method: direct sow early spring or indoor start
bloom_color: deep maroon-black with white stamens
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — may overwinter in zone 7+ mild climates
variety_notes: Also called Pincushion Flower or Mourning Bride. One of the darkest flowers available — nearly black maroon. Honey-scented. White stamens create speckled "pincushion" appearance. Cool-season hardy annual — starts blooming early. Excellent in cottage-style and moody bouquets. Reseeds readily.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: Premier dark flower alongside Bachelor's Button Black Ball and Chocolate Cosmos.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost (cold treatment helps)
bloom_color: deep violet-blue
overwintering_method: Perennial in zones 4-9 — overwinter in garden with light mulch
variety_notes: Larger-flowered perennial pincushion. Blooms first year if started early. Produces continuously from early summer to frost if deadheaded. One of few true-blue cut flowers. Long-lived perennial. Divide clumps every 3-4 years.
source_notes: Different species from annual Scabiosa atropurpurea — perennial behavior changes the planning calculus.

start_method: direct sow early spring (taproot — resents transplanting)
bloom_color: clear sky blue
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — fall plant in zone 7+ for early spring bloom, else early spring direct sow. Reseeds prolifically.
variety_notes: Also called Love-in-a-Mist. Ethereal feathery foliage with clear blue star-shaped flowers. Seed pods ALSO used as cut flowers/dried pods — harvest when inflated but still green. Double-duty plant. Cool-season — bolts in heat. Cannot be transplanted (taproot) — direct sow only. Reseeds reliably. One of few true-blue garden flowers.
sources: Floret Library; Baker Creek; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Seed pod is often more valuable than the flower for cut-flower designers.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost (first year); divisions in subsequent years
bloom_color: mix: white, pink, rose, red, yellow, apricot
overwintering_method: Hardy perennial — cut back to ground in late fall. Divide every 2-3 years. Spreads via runners (contain if needed).
variety_notes: Flat-topped clusters of tiny flowers — excellent flat "plate" form for bouquets. Long-lasting fresh and dried. Colorado mix gives broad color range. Drought-tolerant and low-maintenance. Attracts beneficial insects. Divide clumps in fall or early spring for free new plants. Blooms first year from early-started seed.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Floret Library; Baker Creek
source_notes: Yarrow is beloved by flower farmers for reliability, longevity, and dual fresh/dried use.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: white petals with yellow centers (daisy-like)
overwintering_method: Short-lived perennial (2-3 years) in zones 5-8; reseeds freely — appears volunteer in subsequent years
variety_notes: Small daisy-like flowers in airy sprays — classic "filler" flower for bouquets. Aromatic foliage (medicinal/culinary history). Productive cutter — single plant yields many stems over weeks. Reseeds reliably. Excellent with roses, dahlias, zinnias as a delicate textural counterpoint.
source_notes: Premier "filler" flower for cutting gardens — essential for bouquet design.

start_method: PURCHASE PLUGS — seed-starting is extremely slow and difficult for home growers
bloom_color: multi-petaled rose-like blooms in white, pink, purple, blue, cream, green
overwintering_method: Annual in cold zones; tender perennial in zones 8+
variety_notes: "Rose of Texas" — fluffy rose-like blooms on tall strong stems. EXCEPTIONAL vase life (2-3 weeks). Considered premium/luxury cut flower. HOME GROWERS SHOULD BUY PLUGS, NOT SEEDS — seed-to-bloom takes 5-7 months and requires specific temperature ranges. Voyage series bred for long stems and commercial cut flower production. One of the most profitable flowers for flower farmers.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds; Floret Library; Sakata
source_notes: Seed germination challenge is critical warning for home growers — plugs are the practical path.

start_method: direct sow early spring or indoor start
bloom_color: ivory cream with pink tones
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — reseeds readily. Fall plant in mild zones.
variety_notes: Also called Pot Marigold. Edible medicinal flowers (petals for salads, skin salves). Soft cream-pink tones unusual for calendula — most varieties are bright orange/yellow. Cool-season — bolts in high heat. Prolific self-seeder. Productive cut flower over long season. Short stems limit vase use but good for posies.
source_notes: Edible/medicinal doubles as culinary herb.

start_method: indoor start 4-6 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: mix: magenta, pink, purple, white, red
overwintering_method: Annual; excellent for drying — harvest in full color and hang upside down
variety_notes: Also called Globe Amaranth. Small papery clover-like "globes" about 1" across — unique texture in bouquets. Heat and drought-tolerant — thrives in hot humid weather. Long vase life fresh and indefinite dried. QIS series bred for cut flower production with taller stems. Prolific producer throughout summer.
source_notes: Excellent filler/textural element — dries beautifully.

start_method: direct sow after frost or indoor start
bloom_color: deep burgundy-red tassels and leaves
overwintering_method: Annual; edible seeds can be harvested for grain
variety_notes: Dual-purpose: ornamental cut flower AND edible grain (Hopi traditional food crop — dark red dye from flowers). Tall plants (4-6 feet) with long upright burgundy plumes or drooping tassels depending on variety. Dramatic in arrangements and landscape. Heat-tolerant. Leaves also edible as greens. Plant is its own statement piece.
sources: Baker Creek; Native Seeds/SEARCH; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Traditional Hopi crop — cultural significance in addition to ornamental and culinary value.

start_method: direct sow after frost
bloom_color: dramatic pendulous deep red-burgundy tassels
overwintering_method: Annual; self-seeds readily
variety_notes: Victorian heirloom. Dramatic CASCADING rope-like red tassels that can reach 2 feet long hanging from the plant. Romantic gothic cottage-garden aesthetic. Provides unique "trailing" texture in arrangements. Works beautifully with dahlias, ranunculus, garden roses for romantic design. Edible grain and greens (also called Inca Wheat).
sources: Baker Creek; Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds
source_notes: Pendulous/cascading form distinguishes from upright Amaranthus cruentus.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost; needs cool (50-60F) germination
bloom_color: spires of fragrant blooms: apricot, white, pink, purple
overwintering_method: Cool-season — plant in very early spring or late fall (zone 7+). Intolerant of heat.
variety_notes: Intensely clove-scented spires of double flowers. Cool-season flower — plant early, finishes before summer heat. Iron series is bred for single-cut production with long uniform stems. Seedlings show "double selector" — pale leaves = double flowers; dark leaves = singles (cull singles for cutting garden). Requires cool temperatures to bloom properly.
source_notes: Cool-season timing and the double-selector trick are critical for success.

start_method: direct sow fall (zones 6+) or very early spring — needs cold to germinate
bloom_color: mix: deep blue, purple, pink, rose, white
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — requires cold stratification to germinate. Fall sowing works best in zones 5+. Reseeds reliably once established.
variety_notes: Annual cousin of perennial delphinium. Tall spires of delicate blooms in classic cool colors including the rare true-blue. Must have cold stratification — either direct-sow in late fall, or chill seeds in fridge for 2 weeks before spring sowing. Cool-season — heat-intolerant. TOXIC if ingested — keep away from pets and children. Dries beautifully for dried arrangements.
source_notes: Cold requirement is commonly missed — unchilled seeds won't germinate.

start_method: direct sow or indoor start after cold stratification (2 weeks in fridge)
bloom_color: apple-green bell-shaped calyxes on tall spikes
overwintering_method: Annual — self-seeds if allowed
variety_notes: Unique upright spikes lined with apple-green bell-shaped calyxes (the calyx is what's ornamental — tiny white flowers inside). Provides distinctive structural element in bouquets. Seeds need cold stratification to germinate. Be careful — plant has small thorns. Dries beautifully — color fades to straw but form holds.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: Cold stratification is essential — many gardeners fail with unchilled seeds.

start_method: indoor start 10-12 weeks before last frost (seeds need light — surface sow)
bloom_color: mix: white, pink, apricot, yellow, orange, red
overwintering_method: Short-lived perennial zone 3-7; usually grown as annual. Fall-plant in zone 7+ for stronger spring bloom.
variety_notes: Iceland poppy — different from California poppy and opium poppy. Crepe-paper petals in pastel colors with black stamens. MUST USE SEARING TECHNIQUE to stop sap: dip stem ends in boiling water 7-10 seconds or sear with flame immediately after cutting, else flowers wilt within hours. Harvest when buds show color but before opening. Cool-season — finishes by early summer.
source_notes: The searing technique is essential — ordinary handling leads to wilted flowers.

start_method: direct sow fall or very early spring (taproot — direct sow only)
bloom_color: mix: soft grays, lilacs, pinks, bicolors
overwintering_method: Hardy annual — fall plant in mild zones; self-seeds abundantly
variety_notes: Shirley poppy — strain of the common European field poppy. Mother of Pearl is the soft-palette version with gray/lilac/pink tones. Gardeners select and cross-pollinate for ghostly palette. Short-lived in vase (3-5 days) — best for garden and photography. Cool-season. Bred by artist Cedric Morris. Reseeds vigorously — once established, returns indefinitely.
sources: Floret Library; Johnny's Selected Seeds; Baker Creek
source_notes: Short vase life is inherent to Shirley poppies — primarily a garden flower rather than cut.

start_method: indoor start 10-12 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: soft light pink
overwintering_method: Annual in cold zones; may survive zone 7+ winters
variety_notes: Single-color Chantilly variant — popular for wedding palette consistency. Open-face azalea form. See Chantilly Mix entry for full culture. Extremely long vase life. Solid-color bulk orders easier for large events than mix.
source_notes: Solid-color versions of popular mixes are valuable for designer/wedding work.

start_method: surface-sow (needs light); indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: chartreuse-green bell-shaped flowers
overwintering_method: Annual — self-seeds readily
variety_notes: Unusual chartreuse-green ornamental tobacco. Tall airy sprays of small dangling bell-shaped flowers — excellent "texture" / filler element for bouquets. Attracts hummingbirds. Fragrant in the evening. More refined than typical Nicotiana — no sticky leaves. Filler flower essential for designer-style bouquets.
source_notes: Green/chartreuse flowers are a specialty niche — designers love them.

start_method: indoor start or divisions
bloom_color: bright pink-magenta fading to rose
overwintering_method: Hardy perennial — cut back in fall, divide every 2-3 years
variety_notes: Heirloom pink yarrow. Bright pink flat-topped clusters. Same culture as Colorado Mix but solid color. Fades gradually as flowers age — each plant shows multiple color stages simultaneously. Dries beautifully. Drought-tolerant and reliable.
source_notes: Older cultivar than modern Summer Pastels series.

start_method: indoor start 8-10 weeks before last frost
bloom_color: deep violet-blue spikes
overwintering_method: Perennial zone 8+; annual elsewhere. Drought-tolerant once established.
variety_notes: Mealycup sage. Long narrow spikes of true-blue flowers. Heat and drought tolerant — productive through hot humid summers. Attracts hummingbirds and pollinators. Reliable cut flower — one of the most dependable blues. Part of most flower-farmer standard plantings.
source_notes: Blue is rare in the flower world — salvia is one of the dependable sources.
